proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Necessity of Atheism” (2017), Brown uses Thomas’s Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) and The Ends of Life (2009) to challenge assumptions of uniformly religious past societies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the accepted manuscript, numbered pp. 5–6 (PDF pp. 6–7), p. 10 (PDF p. 11), and p. 13 (PDF p. 14). Brown places Thomas at the start of a “sophisticated historiography sceptical of enchantment”, quotes his “continuity of popular scepticism”, and uses his account of practical attachment to earthly life. Notes 18, 22, 40 and 59 identify the works. The 1978 Penguin edition is explicitly identified as a reprint of the 1971 book. Thomas’s originals remain unread; this is Brown’s documented argumentative use, not a supervision or personal-contact claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Postmodernism for Historians (2005), Brown advocates postmodern interpretation while retaining empirical source checking and questioning neutrality in historical narration.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed preview, Introduction pp. 2, 7, 10–11: “Neutrality is impossible” accompanies the requirement to “conduct empirical research”. These primary passages answer the earlier unread-body hold. Chapter 8 remains unread. Existing culture edge_2863 does not state this epistemological position.

review.reason: Preview Introduction pp. 10-11 found verbatim (checking sources that verify the facts; subjectivity in selecting events and sources; neutrality impossible). Accurate and bounded to 2005.

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'The Agency of Women in Secularization' (2022), a review essay on Philip Jenkins's Fertility and Faith, Brown restates his argument from Religion and the Demographic Revolution (2012) that women's changing fertility choices, higher education, employment and autonomy were central to religious decline from the 1960s, and calls for more attention to the drivers of female employment and the collapse of the ideology of female domesticity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Accepted manuscript read: unnumbered body, especially PDF pp. 5–6 and 8–9 (PDF p. 1 is the repository cover). On PDF p. 6 Brown relates educational and employment opportunities to women’s movement away from organised religion; on PDF p. 8 he calls for more attention to the “economic, individualistic and cultural drivers of female employment and declining religiosity” and the changing ideology of female domesticity. He critiques and welcomes Philip Jenkins’s Fertility and Faith (2020); Jenkins’s book remains unread. This is Brown’s interpretive argument, not independently established universal causation. Distinct from the existing general methods edge to culture and comparative Canadian religion edge. Repository publication date is 2022; 2021 in the DOI and deposit date is not used as the article’s publication year. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Accepted manuscript (Glasgow repository; cover cites Religion, Brain and Behaviour 12(4) 2022) read in full. The argument is supported, but the piece is a review essay on Jenkins's Fertility and Faith, and the education/employment/fertility argument is Brown restating his own Religion and the Demographic Revolution (dated 2012 in n. 10, 2014 in the text). Say that it is a review essay and a restatement.]
